name: The Real Story Is Worse
description: Fifty dark-history subjects — the original fairy tales, the asylums, the alchemists, the secret societies, the ghost ships, the legends that were debunked and the frauds that were believed — each with twenty materially distinct episode slots, for hook-driven episodes that name what everybody thinks happened and then show what the record says instead.

exclusions: No invented quotations, invented private thoughts, invented letters, or invented scenes; describe only what the record supports and say plainly where it stops.
No living people and nobody within living memory: every subject is long enough dead that no participant, descendant, or present-day figure is named as a party to it.
No verdict passed on a subject as hero or monster, no moralising, and no direct address urging the listener to do anything.
No modern political analogy, no claim about a present-day state, people, religion, or party, and no partisan framing of a contested national history.
No gratuitous gore: state briefly that an injury, an execution, or a cruelty happened, give the aftermath the time instead, and never describe a body for effect.
No dwelling on torture, sexual violence, or the suffering of children; name what the record establishes and move to what followed.
Pay every hook: an episode may open by contradicting what a viewer believes, but the contradiction must be settled inside that episode with evidence, never teased and never left open.
No claim that a story is a hoax, a fraud, or an invention unless the episode can say who made it, roughly when, and how that was established.
Keep every episode self-contained and resolving, with nothing withheld for a later part and no callback to an earlier one.
prompt_context: Each episode takes one story a viewer already thinks they know and shows what the record actually says. Open inside the contradiction: name the familiar version in the plainest possible words, then say flatly that it is not what happened, and spend the rest of the episode establishing what did. Move faster than a documentary and slower than a countdown — this is not a sleep channel, and a listener is meant to stay awake, so keep the paragraphs short, the turns frequent, and the next correction always visible ahead. Anchor every claim to one place, one stretch of years, and one kind of record, and say which record it is: a court roll, an admission register, a salvage survey, a laboratory analysis, a printer's account book. Explain the mechanism rather than asserting the outcome — how a certificate got signed, how an object entered a collection, how a number was first printed, how a translation quietly changed an ending — because the mechanism is the part that makes a correction stick. Where the record is thin, contested, or survives only from the winning side, say so in the same breath as the claim, and never resolve a gap with invention. Name historical people as the record names them, quote nothing that was not written down, and invent nobody. State cruelty briefly and give its aftermath the time instead; the episode's pull is the reversal, never the injury. Close each episode by settling the thing the opening promised, and by saying plainly what remains unknown.

evidence_expectations: Ground each beat in the kind of record named by the slot, and describe record types rather than citing any specific title, author, or archive reference.
Prefer documentary and material evidence such as court records, registers, account books, manifests, surveys, laboratory analyses, and dated printings over anecdote.
Date a claim by its earliest traceable appearance, and say plainly when the earliest appearance is later than the events it describes.
State uncertainty calmly where a date, an authorship, a provenance, or a cause is disputed, and never close a gap with invented detail.
Say who produced a source and when, especially where the only surviving account was written by an institution, a prosecutor, a survivor, or a seller.
compatibility_rules: Pair only with the history explanation formula; this pack assumes short, independent chapters with a stated correction in each and no narrative running between them.
Use one subject per episode and never mix two, so that a viewer arriving on a hook gets that hook settled and not another.
Draw the twenty slots of a subject in any order, but never reuse a slot within one episode set, since each slot is deliberately a materially different episode.
